articles.title: Vietnam utility EVN asks renewable developers to negotiate lower tariffs over construction acceptance delays - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam utility EVN asks renewable developers to negotiate lower tariffs over construction acceptance delays  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
State utility Vietnam Electricity's (EVN) power trading unit has asked renewable energy developers to negotiate lower electricity prices for periods when their projects were already in commercial operation but had not received written approval for construction acceptance inspections.
Electricity Power Trading Company (EPTC) asked affected developers to negotiate the maximum possible reduction in power prices for periods when their projects had issues related to acceptance inspections, according to a recent notice.
The negotiated prices should not exceed the ceiling tariffs set for transitional renewable energy projects, EPTC said.
Under the Industry and Trade Ministry's Decision 21/2023, the ceiling prices, excluding value-added tax, range from VND1,184.9 (4.55 U.S. cents) to VND1,508.27 (5.8 U.S. cents) per kilowatt-hour for solar power projects and from VND1,587.12 (6.1 U.S. cents) to VND1,815.95 ($6.98 U.S. cents) for wind projects, depending on the project type.
The actual tariff for each plant will be determined through negotiations between EVN and the developer.
EPTC has asked affected developers to submit their proposed tariffs and supporting documents and arrange negotiation schedules with the company.
Dispute involves 172 renewable power projects
The request follows a 2023 State Audit conclusion, regulations governing solar and wind power development, and a 2024 government resolution aimed at addressing problems with renewable energy projects.
According to the Industry and Trade Ministry, 172 grid-connected wind and solar power plants, or parts of plants, had entered commercial operation without written approval for acceptance inspections at the time of commercial operation or during periods when they were eligible for feed-in tariffs.
A 2023 government inspection concluded that the issue had caused losses for EVN. Several projects were subsequently delayed in receiving payments or received only partial payments under their power purchase agreements.
The ministry later proposed that EVN and developers review the projects' eligibility for feed-in tariffs. For projects that did not fully meet the requirements, the ministry proposed determining revised tariffs and seeking approval from relevant authorities to offset the resulting difference in power payments. The approach was intended to limit disputes while reducing the impact on Vietnam's investment environment.
Developers, however, have challenged the basis for changing the recognized commercial operation dates and tariffs.
They argue that regulations in force when some of the projects began commercial operations did not require written acceptance approval as a condition for achieving commercial operation.
The developers said Circular 10/2023 introduced the requirement for acceptance documentation before an electricity operating licence could be issued. Many of the affected plants had already entered commercial operation in 2021 or earlier.
The developers have therefore called for their recognized commercial operation dates to remain unchanged. They also want the rules applied without retroactive effect and electricity payments made in full under their existing power purchase agreements.
They argue that any breach of construction acceptance rules should be dealt with through penalties and corrective measures. Such breaches should not alter a project's commercial operation status or its contractual right to receive payment for electricity generated.

Coffee prices today, October 5, 2026
 World coffee prices rose across the board last week.
 Over the past week, robusta coffee futures contracts for November 2026 delivery on the London exchange rose 3% ($102/ton) to $3,469/ton. The January 2027 contract increased 3.2% ($106/ton) to $3,448/ton.
 Meanwhile, the price of Arabica coffee on the New York exchange for March 2027 delivery also increased by 3.4% (9.3 US cents/pound), reaching 280.5 US cents/pound. The May 2027 contract increased by 3.3% (8.9 US cents/pound), reaching 277.8 US cents/pound.
 Traders say the recent recovery is mainly due to short covering. Data released by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) shows that in the week ending September 29, speculators reduced their short positions in arabica coffee futures on the ICE US exchange. Accordingly, net short positions in arabica coffee decreased by 2,978 contracts, to 3,493 contracts.
 The upward trend last week was also due to the fact that most of the old crop's inventory had been depleted, while the new crop's supply is still a few weeks away from appearing.
 Meanwhile, the market is closely monitoring weather developments in Brazil as well as factors that could impact global coffee supply. Regular rainfall in Brazil is crucial for coffee flowering. However, the most unpredictable factor currently is El Niño, which is predicted to be one of the strongest El Niño events ever recorded. El Niño can cause adverse weather patterns such as floods, droughts, and temperature fluctuations, thereby negatively impacting coffee production, particularly in Asia, Central America, and South America.
 The Climate Prediction Center of the U.S. National Weather Service forecasts a 75% chance that El Niño will continue until early 2027. The intensity and timing of El Niño will determine the extent of its impact on coffee production.
 On September 30th, certified arabica coffee inventories at New York exchange warehouses decreased by 290 bags, to 260,364 bags. At the same time last year, inventories were more than double the current level. Since the beginning of the year, inventories have decreased by over 40%. For robusta coffee, certified inventories at the London exchange decreased by 32,000 bags, to 864,000 bags.
 Domestic coffee prices also increased slightly last week, fluctuating around 94,000 VND/ounce. Although they edged up, the increase in domestic coffee prices was still significantly lower than in the international market.
 The Vietnamese coffee market remained generally quiet this week due to the depletion of existing coffee stocks from the previous harvest, while new coffee supplies are still a few weeks away. However, traders reported that domestic green coffee prices have edged up.
 Vietnam officially begins its new coffee crop season this Thursday, but traders say it's unlikely that large quantities of the new crop will be available on the market before early November. Traders say the price of the upcoming harvest remains uncertain and difficult to predict. Prices will depend on several factors, including developments in Brazil and weather conditions in the Central Highlands of Vietnam next month. However, current conditions are favorable for coffee cultivation.
 According to data released by the Vietnam General Statistics Office, Vietnam exported 1.45 million tons of coffee in the first nine months of 2026, a 16.2% increase compared to the same period last year. However, the export value of coffee during this period decreased by 7%, to $6.6 billion. In September alone, Vietnam exported 124,000 tons of coffee, a 53% increase compared to the same period last year.

articles.title: Singapore's digital economy is experiencing strong growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Singapore's digital economy is experiencing strong growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to the Singapore Digital Economy Report 2026, released by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) on October 5th, the size of Singapore's digital economy is projected to increase from S$136.5 billion in 2024 to S$144.1 billion in 2025. This growth rate of 5.6% is significantly higher than the 3.1% increase in Singapore's nominal GDP during the same period. The digital economy's share of GDP is also expected to rise from 18.8% to 19.3%.
 The demand for technology professionals has increased rapidly in recent years. Specifically, the number of technology professionals in Singapore is projected to reach approximately 222,200 in 2025, a 3.8% increase from 214,000 in 2024. Currently, the technology workforce accounts for 5.4% of Singapore's total workforce, up from 5.3% in 2024 and 5.2% in 2023.
 Notably, the driving force behind job growth in the technology sector is shifting strongly toward traditional industries. By 2025, the number of technology professionals working in industries outside of information and communication technology (ICT) is projected to increase by 5.3%, to 130,900. Meanwhile, the number of technology professionals within ICT itself is expected to increase by 1.8%, to 91,300.
 Thus, approximately 59% of Singapore's technology professionals currently work outside the technology sector, particularly in fields such as finance, manufacturing, and commerce. This indicates that technology is increasingly becoming a core competency of the entire economy , rather than being concentrated solely within technology companies. Occupations related to artificial intelligence (AI), data, and cybersecurity are among the fastest-growing sectors in terms of workforce. 
 AI is increasingly being adopted by Singaporean businesses. Along with the expansion of the digital economy, the level of AI adoption by Singaporean businesses has also increased significantly.
 According to IMDA, the percentage of businesses applying AI will increase from 14.7% in 2024 to 23.5% in 2025. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), this rate will increase from 14.5% to 23.4%; while for large domestic enterprises, it will increase from 62.5% to 70.4%.
 Nearly 90% of businesses that have adopted AI are using commercially available AI tools, while a segment of businesses are beginning to choose or develop AI tools tailored to their specific needs. Notably, 87.6% of businesses using AI reported that the technology helped improve productivity and streamline processes, while 44% noted positive impacts on cost reduction and resource optimization.
 Digitalization is spreading to traditional economic sectors, a notable point in the IMDA report, noting that much of Singapore's digital economy value no longer comes directly from the technology sector. By 2025, digitalization in sectors outside of information and communication technology (ICT) is projected to generate approximately S$97 billion in added value, a 3.6% increase from S$93.6 billion in 2024. Finance and insurance will lead with S$39.1 billion, followed by wholesale trade with S$29.3 billion. Meanwhile, the ICT sector itself will generate S$47.1 billion in added value, up from S$42.8 billion in 2024. This sector currently accounts for 6.3% of Singapore's GDP, up from 5.9% a year earlier.
 These figures show that digital transformation is taking place on a wide scale, from finance, manufacturing, and trade to service industries, thereby creating additional demand for AI, data, computing, and cybersecurity professionals.
 Tech salaries continue to remain high. These high salaries also reflect the strong demand for tech professionals. The average monthly salary for tech workers in Singapore is projected to reach approximately S$8,000 in 2025, a slight increase from S$7,950 in 2024 and significantly higher than the average S$5,000 for Singaporeans in general. This indicates that tech skills, particularly in AI, data, and cybersecurity, are increasingly valuable in the Singaporean job market.
 Singapore is increasing investment in AI training. Faced with a growing demand for technology professionals, Singapore is stepping up training and skills development for its workforce. The IMDA (Integrated Development Authority of Singapore) stated that its TechSkills Accelerator program will be expanded, aiming to enhance the AI skills of 40,000 technology professionals over the next three years, focusing on advanced AI skills, including agent AI.
 In addition, as part of the National AI Impact Programme, Singapore aims to train approximately 100,000 professionals outside the technology sector by 2029 in specialized AI skills.
 According to Mr. Cao Xuan Thang, Vietnam's Commercial Counselor in Singapore, the rise of the digital economy, AI, and the demand for technology personnel shows that Singapore is shifting from building digital infrastructure to applying technology extensively throughout its entire economy. Notably, the growth driver is not only coming from technology companies but increasingly from traditional sectors such as finance, manufacturing, and trade. This could further fuel investment in AI, data, cybersecurity, automation, and human resource training in the coming years.
 With the digital economy accounting for nearly one-fifth of its GDP, Singapore is consolidating its position as a key regional hub for digital economy and AI, while creating a favorable ecosystem for technology companies, traditional economic sectors, and a highly skilled digital workforce.
 To leverage Singapore's advantages and accelerate the digitalization of its economy, Vietnam should strengthen cooperation in innovation, digital transformation, applied research, and the development of shared laboratory systems. Simultaneously, it should enhance the sharing of human resources in the technology sector to enable Vietnam to quickly integrate more deeply into regional and global supply chains.

Kuala Lumpur (VNA) – Shan Saeed, Chief Economist at Malaysia-based property technology group IQI Juwai, said the latest economic figures of Vietnam have surpassed his earlier forecast of 7–8% growth for 2026 and warranted an upgrade to its growth outlook. 
Vietnam’s GDP grew 9.95% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, well above the median forecast of 8.65% in a Bloomberg survey, bringing nine-month growth to 9.01%. 
Among ASEAN’s “Fabulous Five”, namely Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, Vietnam demonstrates how industrial depth and effective investment can underpin rapid growth, he said, noting strong investment momentum. 
He cited the National Statistics Office under the Vietnamese Ministry of Finance as reporting that total disbursed investment across society surpassed 3.1 quadrillion VND (119.2 billion USD) in the first nine months, up 15.1% year on year, compared with 11.6% in 2025. 
Manufacturing and construction remained the main growth drivers, with third-quarter GDP growth accelerating to 9.95% year on year, from 8.15% in the first quarter and 8.81% in the second quarter. 
Foreign investors are also turning commitments into actual operating capacity. Registered FDI reached 50.36 billion USD in the first nine months, up 76.4% year on year, while disbursed FDI hit 21.07 billion USD, the highest nine-month figure in five years. Manufacturing and processing attracted the largest share of newly registered FDI, at 13.38 billion USD, or 45.8% of the total. 
Saeed forecast Vietnam’s fourth-quarter growth at 9–10% year on year, making annual growth of above 9% increasingly achievable. 
Infrastructure development, manufacturing momentum and domestic consumption would support the outlook, he said. 
Macroeconomic stability remains a key test. Vietnam’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.62% month on month in September, while average CPI increased 4.52% in the first nine months and core inflation rose 4.26%. 
Meanwhile, total foreign trade reached 888.02 billion USD in the first nine months, up 30.4% from a year earlier. Exports rose 24.5%, and imports increased 36.7%. 
The economist said Vietnam’s opportunity lies in turning the current investment wave into sustained productivity gains. Capital is driving the expansion, disbursement is demonstrating its momentum, while policy discipline will be key to sustaining it./.

articles.title: Vietnam GDP set to surpass Thailand in size by 2030 - thethaiger.com
articles.summary: Vietnam GDP set to surpass Thailand in size by 2030  thethaiger.com
articles.full_text:
Vietnam GDP projections now put the country ahead of Thailand when economic size is adjusted for purchasing power and on course to overtake it in nominal terms by around the end of the decade.
But Thailand remains considerably richer per person, meaning overtaking it in economic size and catching it in prosperity are two very different milestones.
World Bank figures put Thailand’s economy at US$577 billion in 2025, compared with US$514.7 billion for Vietnam. Yet Vietnam expanded 8% that year, while Thailand grew 2.4%.
That difference in momentum is expected to continue in 2026. The International Monetary Fund forecasts Vietnam to grow 7.1% this year, compared with just 1.5% for Thailand, the weakest projection among major Southeast Asian economies.
Vietnam pulls ahead on economic size
The balance has already shifted when measured by purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts for differences in local prices. IMF projections put Vietnam’s PPP-based economy at US$2.025 trillion in 2026, making it Southeast Asia’s second largest behind Indonesia and placing it ahead of Thailand.
By 2031, the IMF expects the PPP difference between the two countries to exceed US$500 billion.
Bangkok Bank’s Bnomics research team has reached a similar conclusion on the broader trajectory. Citing IMF projections, it said Thailand could fall to fifth place among Southeast Asian economies by 2030 as both Vietnam and the Philippines move ahead.
Vietnam’s GDP rise does not, however, mean Vietnamese people have become wealthier than their Thai counterparts.
Thailand still richer per person
World Bank figures for 2025 put Thailand’s nominal GDP per person at US$8,056.60, around 59% higher than Vietnam’s US$5,066. When adjusted for purchasing power, Thailand remained ahead at US$26,250 per person compared with US$18,088.50 in Vietnam.
GDP per person is not a complete measure of household welfare or quality of life, but it illustrates why the rankings for total economic size and individual prosperity can move at very different speeds.
Vietnam nevertheless crossed another development milestone in July, when the World Bank upgraded it from lower-middle to upper-middle-income status after decades of rapid expansion following the Doi Moi economic reforms launched in 1986.
For its next target, Vietnam aims to reach high-income status by 2045, and the World Bank estimates that doing so would require average per-capita GDP growth of around 6% a year for the next two decades, alongside a move towards higher-value manufacturing and services, stronger skills, technology and innovation.
Governance becomes the harder test
How Vietnam governs that transition is likely to matter as much as how quickly its factories and exports expand.
Bangkok Bank’s Bnomics team argues that Vietnam has benefited from policy continuity under its one-party political system and the state-directed market model developed since Doi Moi.
Its analysis contrasts that continuity with repeated changes in direction in Thailand and slower progress on programmes including Thailand 4.0 and the Eastern Economic Corridor.
However, the World Bank has warned that the next stage of Vietnam’s development will require stronger institutions rather than growth alone. It has called for more predictable regulation, better public investment, a more capable and accountable civil service and conditions that allow private businesses to become stronger drivers of productivity.
Other analysts have pointed to a further complication. Do Khuong Manh Linh of Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh National Academy of Politics wrote that the Communist Party’s long-running anti-corruption campaign has helped reinforce public trust but has also made some officials reluctant to approve major projects for fear of later scrutiny, contributing to bureaucratic delays.
Thailand faces its own slowdown
Thailand, meanwhile, faces structural pressures of its own. The IMF expects growth of only 1.5% this year, while the Bank of Thailand reported household debt equivalent to 86.7% of GDP at the end of 2025. Thailand’s economy grew just 1.9% year on year in the second quarter of 2026 as household consumption weakened.
Vietnam therefore looks increasingly likely to pass Thailand in overall economic size if current trends continue. Closing the much wider difference in income per person is another matter, and will depend on whether rapid expansion can be converted into higher productivity, stronger domestic businesses and sustained improvements in living standards.
For Thailand, its existing advantage in income per person remains substantial, but slower economic expansion means that the lead cannot be assumed to last indefinitely.

articles.full_text:
Foreign direct investment (FDI) flows into Ho Chi Minh City are showing a clearer shift in terms of sectors and quality. Besides manufacturing projects, many investors are now interested in logistics, seaports, digital infrastructure, high technology, and high value-added services, aligning with the city's new development direction.
Many large projects are turning to infrastructure and technology.
In early September 2026, the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Finance issued an Investment Registration Certificate to Tokgistic Pte. Ltd., an investor from Singapore , to implement the Swift Logistics Company Limited project in Ho Chi Minh City.
The project has a total registered investment capital of over VND 25,850 billion, equivalent to USD 980 million; of which, the investor's contribution is USD 196 million, accounting for 20% of the total investment; the expected capital to be raised is USD 784 million. The project has an operating period of 50 years and is expected to implement its operational objectives from November 2026.
This is one of the large-scale projects newly approved in Ho Chi Minh City this year, demonstrating the growing interest of foreign investors in the logistics sector and services related to the supply chain.
Earlier, in early April 2026, TikTok Shop Vietnam was also recognized among the newly approved FDI projects in Ho Chi Minh City with an investment capital of $125 million. This project is one of the concrete results of discussions between TikTok and the leaders of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee regarding plans to expand operations and strengthen its investment presence in the city. These two projects alone bring the total registered investment capital to approximately $1.1 billion.
Besides the projects mentioned above, Ho Chi Minh City has also attracted many large-scale FDI projects or proposed capital increases this year. Notably, the Can Gio International Transshipment Port project, with a total investment of over US$4.9 billion, is a prime example. The project is expected to enhance international cargo transshipment capacity, expand maritime connectivity, and create further impetus for the development of logistics, trade, transportation, and supporting service industries.
Alongside this is the AI Factory Data Center project with a total investment of approximately $2.1 billion and a proposed capital increase of approximately $2.8 billion. The project is expected to supplement the computing, storage, and data processing infrastructure capacity, serving artificial intelligence applications, digital transformation , and innovation.
In addition to newly approved projects, investors proposed an additional approximately US$2.8 billion for the International University Urban Area Project and approximately US$1.4 billion for the Smart Complex Project in Functional Area 2a of the Thu Thiem New Urban Area. These proposals demonstrate the need for continued investment and development of large-scale projects in the city.
In Ho Chi Minh City's High-Tech Park, FDI flows are also concentrating on areas such as data infrastructure, smart electronics manufacturing, and high-tech services.
You may also like
According to Mr. Nguyen Ky Phung, Head of the Management Board of Ho Chi Minh City High-Tech Park, in the first nine months of 2026, the High-Tech Park granted licenses to two new FDI projects with a total registered capital of nearly 590 million USD, accounting for approximately 48% of the total newly licensed capital. These include the Evolution Wholesale Data Center project with a registered capital of nearly 509 million USD, adding significant investment to data infrastructure; and the Techtronic Tools Vietnam Factory project with a registered capital of 81 million USD, focusing on the production of smart electronic devices.
Representatives from the Ho Chi Minh City High-Tech Park Management Board stated that, when implemented and operated according to schedule, the projects could create additional demand for technology services, highly skilled human resources, and business linkages. These conditions contribute to the development of the science and technology ecosystem and digital transformation in line with Resolution No. 57-NQ/TW; the specific contribution to the city's economic growth should be assessed based on actual performance.
The structure of the projects shows that international capital flows are expanding into sectors such as seaports, logistics, digital infrastructure, high technology, education , research, and high-quality services. These are also areas that align with the investment attraction orientation of the Central Government and Ho Chi Minh City in the spirit of Resolution 10-NQ/TW on the development of the economy with foreign investment.
Creating new opportunities to attract high-quality FDI.
According to Mr. Nguyen Cong Vinh, Vice Chairman of the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City, in the first nine months of the year, the city attracted over US$17.8 billion in FDI, 4.2 times higher than the same period last year. This is a positive sign of business confidence in the city's investment environment, in the context of mechanisms and policies being streamlined and strongly decentralized by the central government.
With these results, Ho Chi Minh City has reached its target ahead of schedule and exceeded the goal of attracting $11 billion in FDI in 2026. FDI projects also contribute to the city's overall economic picture. According to the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, the GRDP for the first nine months of 2026 increased by 9.06%; excluding the oil and gas sector, the GRDP increased by 9.16%. Total social investment capital mobilization reached VND 541,600 billion, an increase of 17.3%.
Based on the results achieved, the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Finance forecasts that the total registered foreign investment capital for the whole year of 2026 will reach approximately US$19 billion, equivalent to 172.7% of the plan and exceeding the US$11 billion target by about 72.7%. This is the projected figure and will continue to be updated according to the investment attraction results in the remaining months of the year. However, along with the scale of capital, the city is placing higher demands on the quality and efficiency of FDI flows.
According to Mr. Quach Ngoc Tuan, Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Finance, the city has recognized that the space for development and attracting FDI through traditional methods no longer has much room for maneuver and has reached a certain limit. Therefore, Ho Chi Minh City is gradually shifting from attracting FDI based on the amount of registered capital to attracting high-quality foreign investment flows.
Notably, the merger of Ho Chi Minh City, Binh Duong, and Ba Ria - Vung Tau opens up a larger development space, creating conditions for the city to shift and change its orientation in attracting foreign investment. In particular, Resolution 10-NQ/TW of the Politburo clearly defines the development orientation of the foreign-invested economic sector, providing a basis for the city to shift from attracting capital based on quantity to focusing on the quality of capital flows.
Representatives from the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Finance stated that the new development space not only expands the scope for attracting investment but also allows the city to shape growth poles with different advantages and development orientations. This, in turn, provides the city with more opportunities to improve the quality of foreign investment flows.
You may also like
To achieve this goal, the city is focusing on improving the investment and business environment, accelerating administrative procedure reforms, and developing policies to attract, encourage, and support investors.
"Based on the Urban Development Law effective from October 1, 2026, the city is also developing policies to attract, encourage, and support investors, including preferential policies to attract foreign investors into sectors consistent with the development orientation. In addition, the city is focusing on developing infrastructure and preparing the necessary conditions regarding location and planning so that investors can quickly implement projects when needed," Mr. Quach Ngoc Tuan stated.
Simultaneously, the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Finance continues to coordinate with relevant departments, agencies, management boards, and localities to monitor and expedite the processing of dossiers for key projects; support existing investors in expanding their operations; and resolve difficulties related to investment procedures and project implementation conditions.
Along with attracting new projects, Ho Chi Minh City also focuses on project implementation, disbursement, and operation; increasing linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises in the supply of goods and services and human resource training.
With this orientation, FDI flows into Ho Chi Minh City are expected not only to increase in scale but also to contribute more to high-tech sectors, logistics, digital infrastructure, green manufacturing, and high value-added industries. This also forms the basis for the city to enhance the efficiency and spillover effects of the FDI sector in the coming period.

Vietnam's GDP grew an estimated 9.01 per cent year on year in the first nine months, with growth accelerating from 8.15 per cent in the first quarter and 8.81 per cent in the second to 9.95 per cent in the third.
As of September 30, total registered foreign investment, including newly registered capital, additional investment and foreign investors' share purchases, reached USD 50.36 billion, up 76.4 per cent year on year.
Additional investment in 948 existing projects totalled USD 14.15 billion, up 25.1 per cent. Real estate attracted USD 6.94 billion, accounting for 16 per cent of total registered FDI.
Disbursed FDI reached an estimated USD 21.07 billion in the first nine months, up 12.1 per cent year on year and the highest level in five years. Of this, USD 1.59 billion, or 7.5 per cent, went into real estate.
The number of newly established real estate businesses rose 10.9 per cent to 4,535 during the period, underscoring the sector's continued appeal as the economy expanded.
Trang Le, country head and senior director of research and consultancy at JLL Vietnam, said international companies' efforts to diversify supply chains were creating additional demand for industrial property.
Companies diversifying supply chains are increasingly looking to Vietnam, driving demand for manufacturing, logistics and related property.
Le added improved transport and logistics infrastructure was also reshaping industrial property, with interconnected manufacturing hubs emerging in both northern and southern Vietnam.
Demand is also expanding beyond traditional manufacturing to electronics, electrical equipment, high technology, automobiles, data centres, pharmaceuticals, research and development, and modern logistics.
Northern Vietnam is expected to add about 5,000 hectares of industrial land by 2030. Haiphong leads the future supply pipeline, with four industrial parks breaking ground in May, while Hanoi has started work on two new industrial parks.
The south is expected to add more than 6,000 hectares by 2030, supported by major infrastructure projects including Long Thanh International Airport, HCM City Ring Road 3 and the Cai Mep-Thi Vai port complex.
Experts said FDI in real estate was not only bringing additional capital into the market but was also tied to expanding production, new facilities and logistics networks, supporting further growth in industrial property.
Efforts to unblock stalled projects
According to Truong Gia Bao, vice chairman and general secretary of the Vietnam Industrial Real Estate Association, Vietnam had made significant changes in its approach, expertise and infrastructure preparations to attract investment.
While foreign investors previously focused largely on Hanoi, HCM City and Danang, they are now considering a wider range of locations and their individual advantages.
Bao noted localities needed to identify the types of investors they wanted to attract, as European, US and Chinese investors differed in their decision-making processes and investment preferences.
Despite rising investment inflows, substantial resources remain tied up in projects stalled by legal obstacles.
According to the Ministry of Finance, 5,012 projects nationwide, covering 213,581 hectares and involving total investment of VND 3.6 quadrillion, are facing difficulties.
Of these, 1,131 projects covering 56,405 hectares and involving VND 779.05 trillion are being handled by ministries and local authorities within their jurisdiction, accounting for 23 per cent of the total.
Another 158 projects covering 13,073 hectares and involving VND 229.41 trillion have been proposed for consideration by the National Assembly, government, prime minister, ministries and other central agencies.
The ministry said most of the remaining projects involved complex legal issues spanning different regulatory periods or specific obstacles that could not yet be resolved under existing mechanisms.

articles.title: Chinese EVs and Global Tariff Responses - Chiang Rai Times
articles.summary: Chinese EVs and Global Tariff Responses  Chiang Rai Times
articles.full_text:
Last Updated on October 6, 2026 by Jeff Tomas
BANGKOK – Chinese electric vehicle exports have grown rapidly, while governments are pushing back over concerns about subsidies, competition, and domestic manufacturing. Tariffs are only one response: some markets also use import quotas or rules designed to encourage automakers to build locally.
As of October 2026, those policies vary widely, and reported proposals shouldn’t be confused with measures that have become law. This guide compares the approaches taken by major markets and considers what they could mean for buyers, automakers, and global trade, including EU tariffs on Chinese electric cars.
Key Takeaways
- The United States applies a 100% Section 301 tariff to Chinese EVs, effective September 27, 2024, on top of ordinary duties, according to the U.S. tariff action.
- The EU adds company-specific countervailing duties to its standard 10% car tariff; rates vary, and EU tariffs on Chinese EVs affect brands differently.
- Canada repealed its 100% surtax in March 2026, replacing it with a quota-limited import arrangement and a 6.1% most-favored-nation tariff for eligible EVs.
- These policies differ in rates, scope, and access conditions, so compare enacted rules and effective dates rather than treating proposals as law.
Chinese EVs and Global Tariff Responses: Why Governments Are Acting
Chinese EV exports have grown quickly enough to reshape competition in major car markets. Governments are responding to concerns about subsidies and domestic industry, while also pursuing supply-chain and manufacturing goals.
How China’s EV export growth raised the stakes
The IEA reported that Chinese electric-car exports doubled in 2025 to more than 2.5 million. China accounted for 70% of global electric-car production and more than 80% of battery-cell production, according to its manufacturing and trade analysis.
That scale can lower production costs, while a strong domestic battery supply chain helps manufacturers secure key components. Together, these advantages let Chinese brands offer competitive prices and expand into overseas markets. Some governments argue that state support, including subsidies, gives Chinese automakers an unfair advantage. Others worry that cheaper imports could put pressure on local automakers and jobs. These concerns have fueled debates over China’s EV subsidies and export strategy, though protecting local industry is not the only motive: governments also want reliable supply chains and investment in domestic production.
What a tariff does to a vehicle’s price
A tariff is a tax on imported goods. If a government applies a 25% import duty to a vehicle valued at $30,000, the duty adds $7,500 before other costs. The final price change may be smaller or larger, however, because companies can adjust prices, exchange rates shift, and shipping or other expenses vary.
Tariffs can cover imports from an entire country or target particular products and firms. A quota sets a limit on how many vehicles can enter, while a local-production rule ties market access or incentives to making vehicles or components domestically. These policies work differently, so compare their actual terms rather than treating them as interchangeable.
How the United States, EU, and Canada are handling Chinese EVs
As of October 2026, the three markets use different rules to limit or manage Chinese EV imports. Their rates and access conditions are not directly comparable: the U.S. relies on a steep tariff, the EU adds manufacturer-specific duties, and Canada limits access through a quota.
The United States keeps a steep 100% tariff barrier
Chinese EVs face a 100% U.S. tariff, which creates a major barrier to direct imports. The U.S. Trade Representative’s tariff determination lists a 100% rate for electric vehicles. That rate should not be treated as the full cost of importing a vehicle or as proof of how every U.S. buyer or automaker is affected. Related U.S. and European trade barriers show how governments have chosen different responses to Chinese manufacturing.
The EU uses duties that vary by manufacturer
The EU’s five-year countervailing duties followed an anti-subsidy investigation and took effect October 30, 2024. The additional rates range from 7.8% to 35.3%, on top of the ordinary 10% car tariff, for a possible combined rate of 45.3%. The European Commission’s duty announcement explains that rates differ by manufacturer. As a result, the added cost depends on the producer, rather than applying one uniform rate to all covered Chinese EVs.
Canada swaps its 100% surtax for a limited import quota
Since March 1, 2026, Canada has allowed an initial annual quota of 49,000 Chinese EVs to enter at the 6.1% most-favored-nation rate. For vehicles within the quota, that replaces the former 100% surtax. Canada administers access in periods, and a second-period import notice took effect September 1, 2026. The government’s Chinese EV quota information tracks the quota period and import limit.
Unlike a blanket tariff, a quota makes access depend on available allocation. Taken together, the policies create different barriers: a high tariff in the United States, company-specific extra duties in the EU, and limited lower-duty access in Canada.
Brazil, Türkiye, Mexico, and other markets are choosing different paths
Outside the United States, EU, and Canada, governments are using a mix of import duties, proposed tariffs, and incentives for local production. Their policies differ in both legal status and the vehicles they cover.
Brazil is restoring EV import duties to support local production
Brazil has reinstated import tariffs on electric vehicles and moved up the schedule for raising duties on semi-knocked-down (SKD) and completely-knocked-down (CKD) kits. The aim is to bring kit imports into line with fully built vehicles and encourage more manufacturing in Brazil. Reports describe changes to the tariffs on EV assembly kits, but exact rates and effective dates for each category are not confirmed here as of October 2026. The measures apply to EV imports generally, not only Chinese-made vehicles.
Türkiye’s reported tariff rate needs careful checking
Reports don’t agree on Türkiye’s additional tariff for Chinese EVs. A 2025 report cited a 40% duty, while an October 2026 analysis listed 50%. Those figures shouldn’t be treated as interchangeable, and the available information doesn’t confirm an effective date for the higher rate. China brought the dispute to the World Trade Organization in October 2025; the WTO’s information on the Türkiye vehicle dispute provides context, but the tariff figures still need careful qualification.
Mexico, the UK, and Southeast Asia show why status matters
Mexico announced a 50% tariff on Chinese and other Asian EVs from January 2026, but implementation details aren’t confirmed here as of October 2026. The UK, by contrast, was reported to be considering duties, which is different from enacting them.
In Southeast Asia, governments have often tied EV incentives to local production or investment commitments. Thailand, for example, has linked tax benefits to domestic manufacturing through EV incentives and production requirements. These policies can shape where automakers build vehicles, but they shouldn’t be described as a verified new China-specific tariff.
What tariffs could mean for EV prices, factories, and trade
Tariffs can change the cost of importing an EV, but their effects depend on how automakers respond. Buyers, factories, and suppliers may all feel the impact, though the available evidence does not quantify the effect of any single tariff on prices, sales, or vehicle choice.
Buyers may see fewer low-cost imports, but the effect is uncertain
A tariff can make an imported model less price-competitive. However, automakers may absorb some of the added cost, raise prices, or change which models they offer. Buyers could then face fewer lower-priced imports, but the size of that effect depends on each company’s pricing and product decisions.
There is no reliable estimate here of how a specific tariff changes consumer prices or sales. The IEA’s global EV policy tool helps compare policy measures, but it does not establish what buyers will pay for a particular vehicle.
Automakers may build locally to keep access to markets
When import barriers rise, companies may consider local assembly, local sourcing, or partnerships to maintain market access and qualify for incentives. Brazil’s renewed focus on EV import duties and domestic production can make local manufacturing more attractive, although the available information does not establish exact effects or company decisions.
Southeast Asian programs offer another example. Thailand has tied EV incentives to production obligations, encouraging participating automakers to match imports with local output. The details differ by program, as described in this overview of Thailand’s EV incentives and local production requirements.
Tariffs can reshape trade without ending competition
Exporters may redirect vehicles toward markets with fewer barriers, while local automakers face pressure to compete on price, features, and technology. Tariffs on finished cars also leave room for continued reliance on imported batteries and components, so they don’t automatically create a domestic supply chain.
Local production can reduce exposure to some import costs, but it may add manufacturing and sourcing expenses. The scale of these changes remains uncertain: available evidence does not show how much tariffs redirect trade, alter competition, or affect component imports.

articles.title: Anchored on Asean: UOB eyes disciplined growth in next decade - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Anchored on Asean: UOB eyes disciplined growth in next decade  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
Its winning strategy banks on regional prospects, wealth, talent and technology
UOB stands on the cusp of a major growth inflection point in its illustrious history.
Fresh from celebrating its 90th anniversary last year, the bank is poised for its next leap as it rides Asean’s growth wave towards its 100-year milestone and beyond. In that time, it has expanded from a local Singapore bank into a regional financial powerhouse.
UOB’s group chief financial officer Leong Yung Chee says the bank is in “a sweet spot to capture the region’s next stage of growth”.
He adds: “Our network spans the region’s most dynamic markets, and we continue to invest in people, capabilities and technology so that we can support our customers better. Our strong capital and liquidity positions provide the resilience as we pursue growth with discipline.”
Asean: Its key growth engine
UOB’s next chapter is firmly anchored in the region’s growing wealth, rising trade flows, and global supply chain shifts.
Asean is set to become the world’s fourth-largest economy by 2030 after the US, China and the EU, with intra-Asean trade growth expected to outpace the global annual average of 5 per cent.
The region remains a strong magnet for foreign direct investment (FDI), attracting a record US$244 billion in 2025, or a 10 per cent rise over 2024.
Leong notes that “Asean stands out as one of the world’s most attractive growth regions, as the world becomes more multipolar and supply chains continue to reconfigure… regional integration is deepening across trade, the digital economy and energy security”.
The bank is in the right place at the opportune time.
Leong says: “Asean has always been our strategic focus. We have built one of the most extensive regional networks, with deep local market knowledge that positions us uniquely to help customers capture the opportunities in the region.”
For instance, UOB has spent over S$800 million in the last decade on an integrated regional platform, building capabilities in payments, cash and trade for its wholesale business.
Unlocking growth and synergies post-Citi acquisition
UOB’s Asean ambitions were boosted in 2022 with its S$4.9 billion acquisition of Citi’s consumer banking businesses in Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam. This deal has significantly strengthened UOB’s regional consumer franchise, which now serves more than eight million customers.
Having completed much of the integration work, UOB is moving towards unlocking value from this enlarged franchise across Asean.
Leong says: “Having stabilised operations, we are now focused on unlocking the full value of our enlarged franchise, particularly in the emerging affluent and affluent customer segments, where we see significant opportunities to drive wealth and main bank relationships.”
The integration has enhanced UOB’s ability to create more value for customers through “expanded product offerings, exclusive partnerships and cross-border capabilities”, he adds.
UOB’s key Asean-4 markets in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam now contribute about 35 per cent of retail banking income and are growing faster than the group.
Its market-leading cards business is also thriving, with higher card billings across Asean. UOB was first in consumer credit card billings for three consecutive years, reinforcing its position as the No 1 card issuer for Visa and Mastercard in Asean.
In the first half of 2026, the bank saw strong wealth momentum across Asean-4, with wealth management income growing 30 per cent year-on-year, led by Malaysia and Thailand.
Overall, Leong notes that the bank is seeing more customers with increased product holdings across deposits, insurance, investments, secured loans and cards.
Winning in wealth and additional priorities
UOB is banking on affluent and emerging-affluent customers as it builds a more diversified, asset-light revenue base post-integration.
Expanding its wealth management business is a core pillar of UOB’s strategy. This is structurally aligned with its Asean long-term growth story and is supported by a large, increasingly affluent consumer base that remains under-penetrated in the region.
Leong says: “Over the next five years, we will double down on wealth by growing our client base, increasing invested assets under management and strengthening advisory-led engagement across our segments, leveraging our regional platforms.”
Supporting these ambitions is UOB’s new long-term strategic distribution partnership with Allianz Global Investors (AGI). By combining UOB’s regional customer reach, advisory expertise, and distribution network with AGI’s global investment capabilities, the partnership will broaden UOB’s wealth offerings and provide customers across Asean with greater access to tailored investment solutions.
This will be supported by “a stronger end-to-end customer experience, combining deeper advisory capabilities with data, digital platforms, and AI to deliver more timely and relevant advice”, Leong adds.
Aside from winning in wealth, UOB has three additional priorities:
- Private bank: Expand with a clear focus on growing AUM and fee income through growing its relationship manager base while broadening regional footprint across North Asia.
- Hong Kong: Renewed growth strategy focused on deepening its capabilities across wholesale banking, treasury and wealth management to help clients expand into Asean, facilitate cross-border trade and investment, and capture opportunities arising from growing regional capital and wealth flows. UOB Private Bank aims to grow Hong Kong AUM and wealth revenue fivefold by 2030 while tripling client advisory headcount.
- Wholesale Banking: UOB’s integrated platforms for payments, trade and cash, and deep sector expertise continue to power growth in trade and transaction banking. The bank will continue to expand its Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA)-light revenue streams through regional connectivity flows.
Future-ready talent equipped with AI tools
UOB is equipping all its staff to deal with the challenges of tomorrow, including AI.
Leong says: “As banking continues to evolve, we are also investing in future-ready capabilities such as AI, data and digital skills, ensuring our people grow alongside the business.”
About 30,000 employees across the group have access to Microsoft 365 Copilot to enhance productivity and simplify everyday tasks. UOB employees already use about 14,000 prompts each day.
Last year, UOB launched its Innovation Academy – a capability-building platform that provides employees with structured learning pathways in areas such as AI, data analytics, blockchain and design thinking. To date, about 90 per cent of the bank’s employees have received generative AI upskilling to strengthen enterprise-wide readiness.
Overall, the bank has a robust track record of investing in its people and developing talent from within.
“We believe strongly in growing our own timber by promoting lifelong learning through reskilling and upskilling programmes,” says Leong.
In 2025, UOB invested S$18.3 million in training, and staff have access to a wide range of upskilling and reskilling programmes to strengthen technical, digital, leadership and cross-border capabilities.
For example, its AI and Data Analytics Centre of Excellence is building capabilities in generative AI and automation to enhance customer experience.
UOB’s approach to AI
Despite AI threatening to disrupt banking and affect jobs, the bank views AI as “an enabler and value creator across banking services rather than a threat to (its) model”, says Leong.
UOB is focused on using AI to improve staff productivity, risk controls and customer outcomes while keeping human relationships, trust and judgement at the core.
Leong says: “Our franchise is built on trusted client relationships and human judgement, particularly in complex, regulated and high-value decisions. AI helps elevate productivity, insight and service quality, but does not replace accountability or trust.”
UOB has leveraged AI across many parts of the bank to strengthen risks and controls, improve productivity, and enable data-driven decision-making.
“Our focus is on using technology to enhance client outcomes (and possible revenue opportunities) while keeping banking relationship-led and advice-driven,” Leong explains.
For staff, its focus is on making AI adoption personal, practical and purposeful, freeing staff from routine work so they can focus on higher-value decisions, creativity and human connection.
The bank has more than 300 AI and data analytics live use cases, in addition to the more than 30 domain-specific knowledge chatbots under the Build-Your-Own-Bot platform, which is designed to help employees obtain information faster and support more efficient decision-making.
This capability also extends to UOB’s Singapore branches, where Branch Bot provides frontline staff with quick access to product information such as interest rates, enabling them to respond to customer enquiries more promptly and effectively.
Leong says: “These use cases touch thousands of colleagues and customers daily, with clear impact – simpler work and higher value delivery.”
UOB has also partnered Accenture to harness GenAI and Agentic AI to transform the bank in Group Wholesale Banking Credit, Anti-Money Laundering and KYC (Know Your Customer), Group Retail Relationship Manager enablement, retail collections and branch experience.
Leading for the next lap
Leading towards 100 years requires good succession planning and bench strength.
Leong says UOB has robust processes to identify and develop talent for senior management positions, and adopts a long-term and sustainable approach to leadership development and succession.
“Other than skills, we emphasise teamwork and a values-based culture,” he shares.
Leong’s optimism about the next 10 years stems from UOB’s resilience and adaptability in the past 90 years, as it successfully navigated multiple economic cycles and periods of uncertainty

articles.title: Singapore: AI-Driven Engineering Advances Sustainable Biomanufacturing - OpenGov Asia
articles.summary: Singapore: AI-Driven Engineering Advances Sustainable Biomanufacturing  OpenGov Asia
articles.full_text:
Singapore has launched the National Centre for Engineering Biology (NCEB) at the National University of Singapore (NUS) to support AI-guided sustainable biomanufacturing and the development of speciality chemicals from renewable feedstocks.
Backed by close to S$50 million (approximately US$38.7 million) in funding over seven years under the National Research Foundation’s Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 plan, the centre brings together universities, polytechnics and public research institutions to strengthen the country’s engineering biology capabilities. Further details are available from the official announcement.
The initiative aligns with wider national efforts to strengthen innovation infrastructure and build a resilient technology base, complementing programmes highlighted in Singapore’s national technology ecosystem strategy. The centre will focus on predictive biological design, AI-enabled experimentation and scalable bioprocessing to support cleaner manufacturing methods and future bioeconomy development.
Developing predictive biological design capabilities
NCEB is hosted at NUS and operates in partnership with Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Institute of Technology, Temasek Polytechnic, Nanyang Polytechnic and the Agency for Science, Technology and Research. The centre aims to move engineering biology beyond largely empirical approaches towards predictive systems capable of modelling how genetic composition influences cell behaviour.
The centre’s work is organised around three research areas: machine learning for predictive biodesign, engineering biology for specialty chemical production, and advanced biofoundry capabilities. Researchers will use AI models, automation and shared data systems to improve the speed and reliability of biological engineering.
Professor Matthew Chang, Executive Director of NCEB, said the centre builds on more than a decade of engineering biology research in Singapore. According to Prof Chang, the objective is to create “more sustainable ways of making products that society depends on, using renewable feedstocks and cleaner manufacturing processes”.
AI and automation supporting sustainable manufacturing
NCEB’s flagship programme focuses on AI-guided engineering biology for sustainable specialty chemicals. These include biosurfactants, specialty lipids, flavour and fragrance compounds, bioactive compounds and advanced material building blocks, many of which currently depend on fossil-derived and energy-intensive production methods.
The programme aims to engineer microbes and enzymes capable of converting renewable feedstocks into specialty chemicals through predictive biological systems. Initial research targets include functional fatty acids used across several industrial sectors.
The approach combines AI-generated biological designs with automated laboratory testing at the Advanced BioFoundry facility. Experimental results are standardised and fed back into AI models, enabling continuous refinement of future designs. The work reflects broader national efforts discussed in Singapore’s AI ecosystem initiatives, which emphasise practical deployment of artificial intelligence in research and industry.
Integrated facilities for design, testing and scale-up
The new NCEB facility at NUS has been structured around a “Design–Build–Test–Learn” workflow. Computational researchers and laboratory teams work in connected spaces intended to shorten the feedback cycle between AI-generated predictions and laboratory validation.
The Advanced BioFoundry serves as the centre’s core experimental platform. Automated systems including robotic liquid handlers, colony pickers, incubators and screening technologies allow large volumes of biological designs to be tested simultaneously. High-throughput analytics systems then assess the output of engineered cells across thousands of samples.
NCEB has also established the Bioprocessing Innovation Platform in partnership with the Singapore Institute of Technology. The platform supports pilot-scale fermentation, downstream processing and production optimisation, helping bridge the gap between laboratory research and industrial manufacturing.
Supporting infrastructure includes several digital platforms: the AI-Augmented Synthetic Biology Database for standardised research data, the Synthetic Biology AI Designer platform for biological modelling, and secure enzyme informatics tools for collaborative analysis.
Building talent and supporting long-term bioeconomy goals
More than 150 researchers, students and professional staff are currently involved across participating institutions, with additional recruitment planned. The centre will also provide research opportunities for undergraduate and postgraduate students.
Long-term objectives include establishing a fully operational AI-enabled engineering biology platform, developing scalable specialty chemical production methods and contributing to international standards in engineering biology. The initiative also supports Singapore’s wider sustainability ambitions, including cleaner industrial processes and innovation-led economic development, similar to goals outlined in Singapore’s sustainable sector transformation efforts.
The launch of NCEB also marks the start of the inaugural Singapore Engineering Biology Week, scheduled from 5 to 8 October 2026. The event is expected to bring together researchers, students and industry participants to discuss developments in engineering biology, research translation and workforce development.

According to a socio-economic report for the third quarter and the first nine months released by the National Statistics Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Finance, Vietnam's GDP grew an estimated 9.01 percent year on year in the January-September period, while third-quarter growth reached 9.95 percent.
Against this backdrop, the country attracted a five-year high in registered FDI, with total registered capital reaching $50.36 billion, up 76.4 percent year on year.
Real estate business remained a major recipient of foreign capital, attracting $6.94 billion in registered capital, including newly registered and additional capital, equivalent to 16 percent of the country's total registered FDI.
The processing and manufacturing sector led FDI attraction with $21.82 billion, accounting for 50.3 percent of total newly registered and additional capital, while other sectors accounted for $14.63 billion, or 33.7 percent.
Despite the strong inflow of foreign capital, the number of newly established real estate businesses also rose, reaching 4,535 in the first nine months, up 10.9 percent year on year.
At the same time, 2,813 real estate businesses completed dissolution procedures, up 123.3 percent from the same period last year.
The construction sector recorded 14,978 newly established businesses during the period, up 33 percent, while 3,646 businesses completed dissolution procedures, a 128.2 percent year-on-year increase.
Across the economy, more than 48,700 businesses completed dissolution procedures in the first nine months, up 118.8 percent year on year.
On average, around 19,100 businesses exited the market each month.
New FDI projects in Vietnam came from 79 countries and territories during the period.
Singapore led investors in newly registered capital with $9.26 billion, accounting for 31.7 percent of the total, followed by South Korea with $5.70 billion, Luxembourg with $4.99 billion, Hong Kong with $3.01 billion, China with $2.27 billion, and Japan with $1.56 billion.
Where is the FDI going?
Experts said international companies' efforts to diversify supply chains and build more flexible production networks are driving demand for new locations, with Vietnam among the countries benefiting directly from the restructuring trend.
This is also one reason behind the strong increase in FDI flowing into Vietnam's real estate sector.
Speaking to Tuoi Tre (Youth) online newspaper on Monday, chairman of the board of directors of ETERNITY Group JSC, a real estate distribution and brokerage company based in An Phu Ward, Ho Chi Minh City, said the FDI inflow into real estate was indeed high, but was concentrated mainly in industrial real estate and several mergers and acquisitions involving high-end projects.
This means the foreign capital has not been distributed evenly across the market.
As a result, many small real estate developers are struggling as they face weak purchasing demand.
"The market has moved beyond the speculative phase toward real estate with real and long-term value. Speculative products such as land plots have therefore weakened. With no new products, weak cash flow and weak purchasing demand, business exits are normal," he said.
Experts also noted that despite the growth in new capital inflows, a large amount of resources remains tied up in projects that cannot yet be implemented due to legal obstacles.
They called for stalled projects to be addressed promptly so that capital and land resources can be put to more effective use.
According to a report from the Ministry of Finance, which serves as the standing body of a government steering committee tasked with resolving problems affecting stalled projects, 5,012 projects nationwide are facing difficulties and obstacles.
These projects cover a combined 213,581 hectares of land and have total investment of VND3.6 quadrillion ($136.7 billion).
Of these, 1,131 projects, with total investment of VND779.047 trillion ($29.7 billion), or 23 percent of the total, are still being handled by ministries, sectors and local authorities within their respective jurisdictions.
Another 158 projects, with total investment of VND229.410 trillion ($8.8 billion), fall under the authority of the National Assembly, the government, and the prime minister.
The Ho Chi Minh City Real Estate Association said that as of September 5, the city still had 1,338 stalled projects facing difficulties and obstacles.
These projects cover more than 30,691 hectares and have a total investment of VND658.084 trillion ($25.1 billion).

articles.title: World Bank Cautious on AI Investment Impact for East Asia’s Economy as Tech Exports Drive Expansion - kaohoon international
articles.summary: World Bank Cautious on AI Investment Impact for East Asia’s Economy as Tech Exports Drive Expansion  kaohoon international
articles.full_text:
The World Bank has revised its 2026 economic growth projection for East Asia and the Pacific upward, attributing the increase primarily to exports linked to artificial intelligence technologies. However, it cautions that the region remains highly susceptible to any reversal in global technology investment trends.
The World Bank’s updated forecast covers 23 economies such as China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand. According to the recent report released on Tuesday, growth in the region is anticipated to reach 4.5% in 2026—an increase of 0.3 percentage points from the April estimate. The expansion will moderate to 4.4% in 2027 and further to 4.3% in 2028.
Among major economies, Vietnam received the largest upward revision, with growth now anticipated at 7.4%, up by 1.1 percentage points.
Much of the region’s export momentum is concentrated in the AI sector. Outside of AI-related categories, trade performance remained marginal or negative. In most countries, over half of export growth originated from AI-linked goods, with this share surpassing 70% in Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam.
South Korea’s official statistics indicated that export value rose dramatically in September to $120.9 billion, largely due to strong semiconductor sales. The World Bank noted that the country’s largest chip companies, Samsung and SK Hynix, together made up 43% of the Kospi index’s market capitalization at the end of April.
On the global stage, the bank commented that AI capital investment has climbed to roughly 6% of U.S. GDP, paralleling the peak during the technology boom of 2000. The current pace of AI investment is more rapid than previous cycles. The Bank for International Settlements has previously observed that the vast scale and speed of the AI surge are reminiscent of past financial bubbles.
The World Bank report also highlighted that much of the financing for AI expansion remains opaque, particularly in private credit markets. It estimates that out of the $2.9 trillion in AI capital spending planned for 2025–2028, $800 billion could come from private credit, a share that grew to 34% of lending activity in 2025 from an 18% five-year average.
Monetary policy tightening is another source of risk; recent interest rate hikes by major central banks—including the first increase by the U.S. Federal Reserve since 2023—could restrain liquidity and investment in the AI sector.
If the AI investment wave moderates, the bank suggests this would not necessarily end the growth cycle, but could indicate investments are currently outpacing realized demand. Historically, a 1% drop in U.S. GDP growth would reduce emerging market expansion by 0.6 percentage points, and would have a greater effect on investments. The region’s extensive role in the AI supply chain means it would be particularly affected by a downturn in AI-related activity.
In Thailand, GDP growth reached an average of 2.4% in 2025 and rose to 2.8% year-on-year during the first quarter of 2026. Nevertheless, expansion eased to 1.9% in the second quarter. Growth was supported primarily by government stimulus, capital spending, and robust export figures, with computers and related components comprising an increasing share of total exports.
Despite these gains, Thailand’s overall manufacturing output contracted, and headline inflation accelerated from negative territory at the start of 2026 to 2.5% in August, primarily because of rising oil prices. Tourist arrivals in the first half of the year dropped to 15.9 million, lower than both the previous year and pre-pandemic levels.
The country also continues to grapple with high levels of public and private debt, as government debt approaches its legal ceiling of 70% of GDP. The bank anticipates growth in Thailand will slow to 2.0% for 2026 and pick up marginally in subsequent years, with elevated inflation and public debt remaining concerns.

articles.title: ASEAN economies grow but young graduates left behind - ABC Asia - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: ASEAN economies grow but young graduates left behind - ABC Asia  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
Across South-East Asia, rapid economic growth has obscured a growing contradiction — while national economies continue to expand, many young people are struggling to achieve economic security, facing persistently high unemployment and a tightening labour market.
Addressing this disconnect requires evaluating how development is conventionally tracked.
ASEAN countries are experiencing respectable GDP growth rates — from 5.1 per cent in Indonesia to 8 eight per cent in Vietnam in 2025.
Yet youth outcomes have not matched the pace of overall growth.
Indonesian youth unemployment remained at 13.1 per cent in 2023, while in Vietnam it grew by 2.8 percentage points between 2010 and 2025 despite GDP per capita more than doubling across the same period.
University graduates feel the pain
High youth unemployment is even more perplexing when placed in the context of rising levels of educational attainment, driven by young people who increasingly pursue tertiary education in line with the conventional wisdom that it offers a path to social mobility.
Yet unemployment among tertiary graduates in the Philippines stood at 3.4 per cent in 2023, higher than the national rate of 2.4 per cent and the rate of 1.9 per cent among Filipinos with only a primary or lower secondary education.
This exemplifies the process of credential inflation, in which the growing supply of degrees outpaces the jobs that require them.
Unemployment statistics may also understate the problem, as jobs with basic social protections and opportunities for advancement are increasingly uncommon.
Informal employment makes up 68.5 per cent of Vietnam’s total workforce. Facing unemployment, some look outwards — 81 per cent of Filipino youth and 79 per cent of Thai youth under 30 expressed willingness to work abroad. This leaves governments with the difficult task of sustaining local employment.
Some academics blame the loss of formal jobs on a decline in manufacturing. In Indonesia, manufacturing value added as a percentage of GDP fell from 32 per cent in 2002 to 19.1 per cent in 2025.
This has negative consequences for labour market dynamics, leading to difficulties in job creation.
Yet the growing investment of ASEAN governments in manufacturing has not translated into a proportionate expansion of employment.
The Indonesian government’s 2020 nickel downstreaming strategy banned raw ore exports to encourage domestic smelting. Yet even as output increased, jobs fell.
The labour multiplier — a measure of the number of jobs supported by a given amount of final demand — decreased from approximately 6514 jobs per Rp 1 trillion ($A80 million) of final demand in 2010 to 3366 in 2016.
Vietnam also planned to invest in semiconductors but faced a severe shortage of skilled engineers.
More automation means fewer jobs
Labour demand shifts further complicate employment outcomes.
Much of the region’s new investment has moved towards capital- and technology-intensive industries that require fewer workers.
A 2018 survey of 150 Indonesian employers struggling to hire found 77 per cent cited the challenge of finding candidates with the desired qualifications.
The International Labour Organization warned ASEAN in 2016 that nearly three in five jobs in the region face a high risk of automation, with the risk reaching as high as 70 per cent in Vietnam.
Governments across ASEAN have begun implementing policies targeted at developing the skills needed for development under changing labour market conditions.
The Philippine government has received over $A1.4 billion in policy loans from the Asian Development Bank since 2017 to support initiatives promoting youth employment, including a program matching young people with internships, work and career guidance. Indonesia also launched its National Internship Program in October 2025.
The problem is that such programs focus on the resources they provide, without considering whether those resources will be converted into meaningful outcomes. An official evaluation of Indonesia’s policy in April 2026 revealed regional disparities and misaligned job roles.
What can be done?
To address the unemployment crisis, policy interventions should focus on converting economic growth into development.
National internship and training programs should focus on the competencies participants can demonstrate upon graduating. Work placement programs should also be designed to offer supervised training in professional judgement and workplace readiness, with skill certifications and reporting of employment outcomes.
Education policies should likewise be judged by the capabilities they build. Schooling must develop skills that will not be made redundant by automation.
With nearly three in five jobs across ASEAN at risk, public spending is better directed at the analytical and cross-disciplinary skills employers already report missing, since the expansion of tertiary education has outpaced the growth of graduate-level jobs.
Strategic investment should also prioritise industries that provide high-quality employment opportunities, a criterion capital-intensive sectors have consistently failed to meet.
Where a large proportion of the workforce is engaged in informal employment, such as in Vietnam, social protections for informal and underemployed workers can help ensure young people have the support to sustainably seek work and drive economic activity.
The ASEAN Qualifications Reference Framework, which enables comparisons of education qualifications across participating member states, could also turn ASEAN’s demographic imbalances into a shared advantage.
While more research is needed on how best to drive youth economic activity in South-East Asia, an over-reliance on GDP as a development proxy creates structural incentives to leave large portions of the population behind. Holistic understandings of development alongside growth must guide ASEAN’s future policymaking.
